note: claude-opus-5-5、入力 3301 / 出力 2767 トークン

data.question: For the quiet season, should we close the utility gap by raising block_k from 2 to 3 (option 2), by setting sanction_lambda from 0.5 to 0 (option 3), by raising hold_limit from 60s to 70s (option 1), or by making no change (keep)?
data.background: Option 2 gives the largest gain that keeps penalties (utility_gap +7.5), but A and B voted it down. It also lowers min_company_on_time_rate and on_time_deliveries, and it reverses D1, which you adopted against the vote on the principle that intersection waiting is no company's right. Weighing that principle against the new fairness KPI is a value judgement I should not make. Option 3 passes every machine check and all three companies voted for it, but it closes the gap by removing the road's sanction incentive, not by changing behaviour. Accepting that risk for later busy seasons is a policy choice that belongs to you.

options.summary: block_k 2 → 3. utility_gap improves by +7.5 (4/5 seeds). On-time falls from 80.8 to 74.8, late rises from 1.8 to 7.8, blocked seconds rise from 1046 to 2396, lowest on-time rate falls from 0.96 to 0.83 (still above the 0.7 floor), road violations fall from 26.0 to 20.6, sanction_total falls from 20.0 to 12.3. Utility A / B / C: 23.0 / 23.6 / 15.9. Votes: × × ○. Adopting it overrides A and B and reverses D1.
options.stakeholders: C gains (utility 10.2 → 15.9). A and B lose (25.2 → 23.0, 25.4 → 23.6). A is the company most blocked at intersections, so it bears the extra waiting. Customers lose: 6 fewer on-time deliveries and 6 more late deliveries. The D1 principle that intersection waiting is no company's right would be given up.

options.summary: sanction_lambda 0.5 → 0. utility_gap improves by +12.0 (4/5 seeds). On-time stays 80.8, late stays 1.8, blocked seconds stay 1046, road violations stay 26.0, lowest on-time rate stays 0.96. sanction_total falls from 20.0 to 0.0. Utility A / B / C: 25.2 / 27.2 / 28.4. Votes: ○ ○ ○. The gap closes because penalties disappear, not because behaviour changes.
options.stakeholders: C gains most (10.2 → 28.4) and B gains (25.4 → 27.2). A is unchanged (25.2) and falls from roughly level to lowest. A also loses its protection if blocking increases once sanctions are gone, especially in busy seasons. Customers see no change in this measurement, but could face more lateness later if road discipline weakens.

options.summary: hold_limit 60s → 70s. utility_gap improves by +1.7 (4/5 seeds). On-time falls from 80.8 to 80.2, late rises from 1.8 to 2.4, blocked seconds rise from 1046 to 1193, road violations fall from 26.0 to 23.6, lowest on-time rate falls from 0.96 to 0.95, sanction_total falls from 20.0 to 19.0. Utility A / B / C: 25.0 / 24.7 / 11.5. Votes: ○ × ○. It can be adopted automatically.
options.stakeholders: C gains slightly (10.2 → 11.5). A and B lose slightly (25.2 → 25.0, 25.4 → 24.7), and B voted against it. Customers lose slightly: 0.6 fewer on-time deliveries and 0.6 more late deliveries. The gap remains large.

options.summary: Stay at v2. On-time 80.8, late 1.8, blocked seconds 1046, road violations 26.0, lowest on-time rate 0.96, sanction_total 20.0. Utility A / B / C: 25.2 / 25.4 / 10.2. The main goal (utility_gap) does not improve.
options.stakeholders: A and B keep their current utility. C stays far behind (10.2), which works against the KPI aim of keeping the companies cooperating. Customers keep the current on-time service.

recommendation.reason: It gives the largest gap reduction (+12.0, 4/5 seeds) and also meets the monitored goal sanction_total (20.0 → 0.0). It changes no delivery metric in the measurement and all three companies voted yes. It also leaves D1's block_k untouched. I recommend it only as a quiet-season measure, with two conditions you should record: re-measure road violations, blocked seconds and A's on-time rate next period, and restore sanction_lambda to 0.5 if blocking rises or when the busy season returns. If you judge that removing all penalties is unacceptable even for one season, choose keep rather than 2, because 2 reduces on-time delivery and overturns the D1 principle against two votes.

unknowns: Whether the companies, especially C, will block more once sanctions are gone; the measurement does not appear to model a change in company behaviour (the delivery metrics are identical to the current state).
Why C's utility is low under the current rules. Its rise to 28.4 when sanctions are removed suggests it bears most of the sanctions, possibly for blocking A, but this has not been confirmed.
How long the quiet season lasts and what demand will be next period.
How customers would perceive weaker road discipline, or the extra late deliveries under option 2.
Why A and B voted against option 2, and why B voted against option 1.
What happens in the 1 of 5 seeds where each option did not improve.
Whether option 1 combined with option 3 behaves differently from either alone; the combination was not measured.
Whether the KPI phrase 'gain or lose because of how the road is used' is meant to treat sanctions as part of road use.
